preamble: The close-mid front unrounded vowel [e] becomes back rounded [o], usually by assimilation to a neighbouring sound with back or labial articulation. Latin backed e to o before w and before velar l (novus, holus < helus); Old Provençal did it before labials (premier > promier); and Russian turned stressed e into o after soft consonants before a hard one (о чём, ёлка). Polish did the same before hard dentals (przegłos: *žena > żona, *nesǫ > niosę).

examples.note: Stressed *e after a soft consonant became o (spelled ё) when no soft consonant followed; hence alternations like ель/ёлка, лечь/лёг.
The historical change is e > o; [ɵ] is the synchronic allophone of stressed /o/ after a soft consonant (o → ɵ).
e became o before velar l.
e became o before a labial, especially m.

Przegłos: *e became o before a hard dental (t, d, s, z, n, ł, r), and the preceding consonant stayed soft; before a soft consonant e was kept, as in żeński 'feminine'. Sources write the law *e > o; modern Polish e and o are pronounced [ɛ] and [ɔ].
Contrast bierzesz 'you take', where r was soft before *e and e stayed.
